origins.name: Austria-Hungary
origins.note: Reported as one empire until 1918 in some years; split into Austria and Hungary in others.

origins.name: England
origins.note: Before 1820, includes the English share of British arrivals estimated by historians.

origins.name: Enslaved, via the Caribbean
origins.note: People already enslaved in the Caribbean and shipped on to North America. Most were born in Africa.

origins.name: Ireland
origins.note: The whole island before 1925; includes Ulster Scots-Irish in the colonial era.

origins.name: Latin America, other or not specified
Not tabulated by country (nonwhite)

origins.name: Russia / Soviet Union
origins.note: Reported as Russia before 1917 and as the Soviet Union until 1991; covers the present-day successor states.

C.label: Historians' estimate
C.long: Period totals from historians (Menard, Tomlins, Fogleman), spread evenly across the years of each period. Enslaved Africans: SlaveVoyages estimates.

W.label: War years · Europeans not estimated
W.long: No estimate exists for European arrivals during the Revolutionary War; the slave trade is shown where recorded.

G.label: Estimated total · origin mix assumed
G.long: About 9,900 Europeans a year (Grabbe, via Cohn). Their origins are assumed to match the 1820s official counts.

H.label: Official total · origins partly estimated
H.band: Official totals; origins from yearly group counts and decade totals
H.long: The yearly total is the official count. Each country's official decade total is spread across the decade following the yearly counts for its country group (Historical Statistics of the US, 1960, series C 88–114).

D.label: Official total · origins split from decade counts
D.band: Official totals; origins from decade counts
D.long: The yearly total is the official count. Origins are official decade totals divided among the decade's years in proportion to the yearly totals.

A.label: Official count
A.long: Persons obtaining lawful permanent resident status, by country of last residence (INS Statistical Yearbook).

B.label: Official count by birthplace
B.band: Official yearly counts by country of birth
B.long: Persons obtaining lawful permanent resident status, by country of birth (INS and DHS yearbooks).

N.label: Not yet published
N.long: The arrivals count for this year has not been published yet.

events.title: Jamestown founded
events.t: English colonists establish the first permanent English settlement in North America, in Virginia.

events.title: First enslaved Africans in English Virginia
events.t: About twenty Africans, taken from a Portuguese slave ship, are sold at Point Comfort, Virginia.

events.title: Plymouth Colony
events.t: The Mayflower lands Separatist Puritans and other English settlers in Massachusetts.

events.title: New Netherland
events.t: The Dutch West India Company begins settling the Hudson Valley; New Amsterdam follows in 1625.

events.title: Great Migration of Puritans
events.t: Roughly 20,000 English Puritans settle Massachusetts Bay over the next decade.

events.title: New Sweden
events.t: Swedish and Finnish colonists settle along the Delaware River.

events.title: England takes New Netherland
events.t: New Amsterdam becomes New York; the Dutch population remains.

events.title: Germantown founded
events.t: German Mennonites and Quakers settle near Philadelphia, opening Pennsylvania to German-speaking migration.

events.title: Ulster migration begins
events.t: Large-scale emigration of Presbyterian Scots-Irish from Ulster to Pennsylvania and the backcountry starts around 1717–1718.

events.title: New Orleans founded
events.t: French Louisiana's capital becomes the main entry point for enslaved Africans to the Gulf Coast.

events.title: Seven Years' War
events.t: War in North America and Europe sharply reduces transatlantic migration until 1763.

events.title: American Revolution
events.t: War halts most immigration and the slave trade until the 1780s.

events.title: Naturalization Act
events.t: Congress limits naturalization to "free white persons" of good character.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase
events.t: The US buys French Louisiana. South Carolina had reopened its slave trade in 1803, and imports surge until 1807.

events.title: Slave importation banned
events.t: The federal ban on importing enslaved people takes effect on January 1, 1808. Smuggling continues on a small scale.

events.title: Steerage Act
events.t: The first federal law regulating passenger ships requires arrival manifests, the basis of US immigration statistics from 1820.

events.title: Irish Famine
events.t: Potato blight causes famine in Ireland (1845–1852); over a million Irish emigrate to the US over the following decade.

events.title: Revolutions in Europe; Mexican Cession
events.t: Failed revolutions push German emigration. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo transfers northern Mexico to the US.

events.title: California Gold Rush
events.t: Migrants arrive from China, Mexico, Chile, Europe and Australia.

events.title: Homestead Act
events.t: Free land in the West attracts Scandinavian, German and Czech farmers.

events.title: Page Act
events.t: The first restrictive federal immigration law, aimed mainly at Chinese women.

events.title: Chinese Exclusion Act
events.t: Chinese laborers are barred from entering; the ban is extended until 1943.

events.title: Ellis Island opens
events.t: The federal immigration station in New York Harbor processes most arrivals for the next three decades.

events.title: Peak year of the great wave
events.t: About 1.3 million immigrants are admitted, mostly from Southern and Eastern Europe. The Gentlemen's Agreement (1907–1908) limits Japanese labor migration.

events.title: World War I
events.t: War in Europe cuts transatlantic migration sharply.

events.title: Immigration Act of 1917
events.t: Adds a literacy test and an "Asiatic Barred Zone".

events.title: Emergency Quota Act
events.t: First numerical quotas by national origin, set at 3% of each group's 1910 population.

events.title: Johnson–Reed Act
events.t: National-origins quotas cut immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe and bar most Asians. The Western Hemisphere stays outside the quotas.

events.title: Great Depression
events.t: Immigration falls to its lowest level since the 1830s; hundreds of thousands of Mexicans and Mexican Americans are pushed to leave.

events.title: Bracero Program
events.t: A US–Mexico agreement brings Mexican contract workers (1942–1964); braceros were temporary workers, not counted as immigrants.

events.title: Chinese exclusion repealed
events.t: The Magnuson Act ends exclusion but sets a quota of 105 Chinese immigrants a year.

events.title: Displaced Persons Act
events.t: Admits about 400,000 Europeans displaced by World War II by 1952.

events.title: McCarran–Walter Act
events.t: Keeps national-origins quotas but ends the racial bar on naturalization.

events.title: Cuban Revolution
events.t: The first of several waves of Cuban exiles arrives in Florida.

events.title: Hart–Celler Act
events.t: Abolishes national-origins quotas in favor of family and skills preferences. Asian and Latin American immigration grows sharply.

events.title: Fall of Saigon
events.t: Refugee resettlement from Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia begins.

events.title: Refugee Act; Mariel boatlift
events.t: Congress creates the modern refugee system. About 125,000 Cubans arrive by boat from Mariel.

events.title: IRCA amnesty
events.t: About 2.7 million unauthorized residents gain legal status. Most of them are counted as new permanent residents in 1989–1991, which produces the spike in those years.

events.title: Immigration Act of 1990
events.t: Raises overall limits and creates the diversity visa lottery.

events.title: September 11 attacks
events.t: Security reforms follow and the Department of Homeland Security takes over immigration services (2003).

events.title: COVID-19 pandemic
events.t: Consular closures and travel restrictions sharply cut new permanent residents in 2020 and 2021.

intro: This atlas follows migration into the territory of the present-day United States for every year from 1607 to 2024. Two measures run through it. Arrivals count the people who came in a given year, by where they came from. Immigrants living in the US count residents born abroad, by birthplace, as censuses and surveys recorded them.

No single record covers four centuries, so each era uses the best source available, and the page marks which kind of number you are looking at. Official counts show as plain figures. Estimates show with a ≈ sign and an outlined marker. Values between census years are interpolated.
caveats: Before 1820 nobody counted arrivals. Colonial figures are historians' reconstructions with wide ranges (for example, 84,500–120,000 Germans arriving 1700–1775). They are spread evenly over each period, so year-to-year changes before 1820 are not real.

Enslaved Africans were brought by force. They are counted from the SlaveVoyages estimates of captives landed directly from Africa, plus documented voyages from the Caribbean. Smuggling after the 1808 ban is undercounted, and the domestic slave trade is internal migration, so it is left out.

From 1820 to 1987 the yearly totals are official, but origins by country were published by decade. Each decade's country totals are spread across its years using yearly counts for broad country groups (through 1957) or in proportion to the yearly totals (1958–1987). Per-country values in those years are shown with a ≈ sign.

Official arrivals record country of last residence through 1988 and country of birth from 1989; the two can differ. From 1892 they count immigrants admitted; since the 1980s they count people granted permanent residence that year, including people already living in the US. The 1989–1991 spike is the 1986 amnesty (IRCA). Unauthorized migration, temporary workers and refugees not yet adjusted are not counted as arrivals.

Country names follow each source. Empires and unions that later split (Austria-Hungary, the Soviet Union, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia) appear under their historical names, so a country's line can start or stop when borders changed.

Census birthplace data begin in 1850 and are interpolated between census years. The 1940 and 1950 censuses tabulated country of birth for white residents only; other foreign-born residents appear as not tabulated.

Arrows start at each origin and end at a schematic point of arrival chosen from where the origin lies: the main East Coast port of the era, Florida, the Mexican border, San Francisco or the Canadian border. Arrows for enslaved Africans end at the landing region SlaveVoyages records. Arrow width grows with the square root of the number of people, on one scale for all years.
The shaded United States shows the colonies, states and territories as they stood on July 1 of the year. Colonies are drawn from their organized counties rather than their sea-to-sea charter claims.
